data.stimulus:
Asymptotic bounds (4%)

Below are a number of running-time expressions. Which running time grows asymptotically slowest?

Exactly one answer is correct, but you may select more than one if you are in doubt.
data.title: Asymptotic bounds (4%)

metadata.distractor_rationale: We compare by simplifying each expression to its dominant term: \[n^2+n \log n=\Theta(n^2), \qquad n^{\log_2 3}+1000\, n=\Theta(n^{\log_2 3}),\] \[n \log n+\sqrt{n}=\Theta(n \log n), \qquad 2^n+n^{100}=\Theta(2^n).\] \[\log(4^n)=n \log 4=\Theta(n).\] The slowest-growing (and hence fastest) one is \(\Theta(n)\), that is, \(\log(4^n)\).

data.stimulus:
Recurrences (4%)

Assume that \(n\) is a power of \(3\) and that \(T(1)=1\). Consider the recurrence \[T(n) = 5\, T(n/3) + O(n \log n).\] What is the solution to the recurrence?

Exactly one answer is correct, but you may select more than one if you are in doubt.
data.title: Recurrences (4%)

metadata.distractor_rationale: Write the recurrence in the form \(T(n)=aT(n/b)+f(n)\) with \(a=5\), \(b=3\) and \(f(n)=O(n \log n)\). We have \(n^{\log_b a}=n^{\log_3 5}\). Choose \(\varepsilon < \log_3(5) - 1\); then \(n \log n = O\bigl(n^{\log_3(5)-\varepsilon}\bigr)\). Hence \(f(n)=O(n^{\log_3 5-\varepsilon})\), and the master theorem (case 1) gives \(T(n)=\Theta(n^{\log_3 5}).\) The other options are therefore incorrect.

data.stimulus:

A recursive algorithm SortAndRule on an input of size \(n\) (a power of 2) consists of three parts:

  • Sorting the input in time \(\Theta(n \log n)\)
  • Four recursive calls on subproblems of size \(n/2\)
  • A combine step that runs in time \(\Theta(n)\)

For input size \(n=1\), SortAndRule runs in time \(T(1)=1\). Which of the recurrences below best describes the running time \(T(n)\) of SortAndRule? (You do not need to solve the recurrences, only determine which one corresponds directly to the algorithm.)

Exactly one answer is correct, but you may select more than one if you are in doubt.
data.title: Divide and conquer (4%)

metadata.distractor_rationale: The four recursive calls on subproblems of size \(n/2\) are expressed by \(4 T(n/2)\). The combine step and the sorting step take total time \(\Theta(n \log n)\), which is added.

data.stimulus:
Loop invariants (4%)

Consider the following algorithm, which takes as input an array \(A[1\!:\!n]\) and a natural number \(n\).

After each iteration of lines 3–4 we still regard the variable \(i\) as unchanged; its value is changed only at the beginning of the next iteration. Which of the following statements is a correct loop invariant of the for loop?

Select one or more correct answers.
data.title: Loop invariants (4%)

metadata.distractor_rationale: We first argue that option 2 is correct. Before a given iteration, the algorithm has already processed the elements \(A[1],\dots,A[i-1]\), so \(m\) contains their maximum. During the iteration, \(A[i]\) is compared with \(m\), after which the invariant again holds for the next iteration. It follows that we always have \(m\geq \min \{A[1],\dots,A[i-1]\} \geq \min \{A[1],\dots,A[i]\}\). The other invariants fail for \(i=2\) if \(A[1]=2\) and \(A[2]=1\) (options 1 and 6) or if \(A[1]=1\) and \(A[2]=2\) (option 5).

data.stimulus:
Running-time analysis (4%)

Let RB-Tree-Create\(()\) denote a procedure that creates a red-black search tree (with no keys) as described in CLRS Chapter 13. The procedure RB-Tree-Search\((x,k)\) searches for the key \(k\) in a red-black search tree with root \(x\) (returning \(T.nil\) if the key is not present), the procedure RB-Insert\((T,z)\) inserts a node \(z\) into a red-black tree \(T\), and the procedure RB-Node\((k)\) creates a node containing the key \(k\).

Consider the following algorithm, which determines whether two arrays \(A[1\!:\!n]\) and \(B[1\!:\!m]\), each containing a sequence of keys (not necessarily sorted), have an element in common.

What is the asymptotic worst-case running time of the algorithm over all input arrays of length \(n\) and \(m\), respectively?

Exactly one answer is correct, but you may select more than one if you are in doubt.
data.title: Running-time analysis (4%)

metadata.distractor_rationale: The first loop inserts \(n\) elements into the red-black tree. Insertion \(i\) costs \(\Theta(\log i)\), so the total is \(\sum_{i=1}^{n} \Theta(\log i) = \Theta(n \log n)\). The second loop performs up to \(m\) searches in a tree with \(n\) keys, so each search costs \(\Theta(\log n)\), and the total is \(\Theta(m \log n)\) in the worst case (if there is no common element). Altogether this gives \(\Theta(n \log n + m \log n)\).

data.stimulus:
Amortized analysis (4%)

Consider dynamic tables as described in CLRS Section 16.4.1 (without deletions), but with the following variant of Table-Insert\((T,x)\), in which the table size is expanded by a factor \(k\), where \(k\geq 2\) is an integer parameter:

Assume that a new table can be allocated in constant time, regardless of its length. CLRS Section 16.4.1 uses the potential function \(\Phi(T) = 2(T.num - T.size/2)\) for the analysis. Which of the potential functions below is best suited for an amortized analysis of Table-Insert\(_k\) showing that the time per insertion is \(O(1)\), independently of \(k\)?

Exactly one answer is correct, but you may select more than one if you are in doubt.
data.title: Amortized analysis (4%)

metadata.distractor_rationale: Expressions with the factor \((T.num - T.size/2)\) can become negative for \(k>2\) and therefore do not give valid potential functions. The expression \(k(T.num - T.size/k)\) increases by \(k\) each time \(T.num\) is incremented by 1, so it leads to an upper bound of \(O(k)\) on the amortized cost. The remaining option is \(\Phi(T) = 2(T.num - T.size/k)\), which works: On an expansion, \(\Theta(T.size)\) elements are copied, so the potential must drop by a corresponding amount exactly when \(T.num = T.size\). With \(\Phi(T)=2(T.num - T.size/k)\) the potential increases by a constant on an ordinary insertion (since \(T.num\) is incremented by 1), which gives constant amortized cost in the cheap cases. When the table is expanded, \(T.size\) changes from \(s\) to \(ks\), while \(T.num=s\). Hence \(\Phi(T') = 2(s - ks/k) = 0\), so the potential drops sharply and pays for the copying.

data.stimulus:
LSM trees (4%)

Consider a simple LSM tree, as described in the note on LSM trees, in which all sorted lists have a length that is a power of \(2\), and in which for each size \(2^i\) there is at most one (sorted) list. What can be said about the number of binary searches (in nonempty lists) that must be performed to search for a key in an LSM tree with \(n > 15\) elements?

Select one or more correct answers.
data.title: LSM trees (4%)

metadata.distractor_rationale: There can be at most one nonempty list of each size \(2^i\), so the number of nonempty lists is at most the number of bits in \(n\), i.e., \(\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor+1 \leq \lg(n+1)\), and this bound is tight. If \(n\) is a power of 2, only one list needs to be searched.

Bellman-Ford (4%)

Consider the following directed, weighted graph \(G\):

We run \(\text{Bellman\text{-}Ford}(G,w,s)\) as described in CLRS Section 22.1, and in each iteration we go through the edges in the order \((s,a),(s,b),(a,b),(a,c),(b,c)\). What are the distances \((d[s],d[a],d[b],d[c])\) after the second full iteration of the main loop (lines 2–4 in the CLRS pseudocode)?

Exactly one answer is correct, but you may select more than one if you are in doubt.
data.title: Bellman-Ford (4%)

metadata.distractor_rationale: Initialization: \(d[s]=0\) and the others are \(\infty\). First iteration: relaxing \((s,a)\) gives \(d[a]=4\), relaxing \((s,b)\) gives \(d[b]=5\), relaxing \((a,b)\) gives \(d[b]=2\), relaxing \((a,c)\) gives \(d[c]=10\), relaxing \((b,c)\) gives \(d[c]=3\), so after the first iteration we have \((0,4,2,3)\). In the second iteration none of the edges can improve these values, so the distances remain \((0,4,2,3)\).

data.stimulus:
Complete the algorithm (4%)

Consider the following algorithm (with an unspecified part), which takes as input an array of integers \(A[1\!:\!n]\) and positive integers \(n\), \(k\). The algorithm must return the largest sum that can be obtained by choosing at most \(k\) elements from \(A[1\!:\!n]\) (an empty sum, with sum \(0\), is allowed), i.e., we must find \(\max_{|I|\leq k}\sum_{\ell\in I} A[\ell]\). The algorithm works by computing an array \(B[0\!:\!n, 0\!:\!k]\), where \(B[i,j]\) is the largest sum \(\sum_{\ell\in I} A[\ell]\) that can be obtained by choosing \(I\subseteq \{1,\dots,i\}\) with \(|I|=j\) elements, or \(-\infty\) if no such set exists.

Which expression should replace “INSERT CODE HERE” to obtain a correct algorithm?

Exactly one answer is correct, but you may select more than one if you are in doubt.
data.title: Complete the algorithm (4%)

metadata.distractor_rationale: When we see \(A[i]\), the best sum with exactly \(j\) chosen elements in the prefix \(A[1\!:\!i]\) can either (1) not choose \(A[i]\), which gives the old value \(B[i-1,j]\), or (2) choose \(A[i]\), which requires that we had previously chosen exactly \(j-1\) elements in \(A[1\!:\!i-1]\), and gives \(B[i-1,j-1]+A[i]\). Therefore the update is \(B[i,j]\gets\max\{B[i-1,j],B[i-1,j-1]+A[i]\}\).

data.stimulus:
Disjoint sets (4%)

We consider tree representations of disjoint sets, as described in CLRS Section 19.3, using the weighted-union heuristic without path compression. Assume that \(n\) and \(m\) are large integers (not bounded by any constant) with \(m < n - 1\). An algorithm makes \(n\) calls to Make-Set and \(m\) calls to Union. What holds for the running time of a call to Find-Set\((x)\)?

Select one or more correct answers.
data.title: Disjoint sets (4%)

metadata.distractor_rationale: The height of a tree with \(k\) nodes is at most \(\log k\) because of the weighted-union heuristic. If we perform \(m\) Union operations, there can be at most \(m+1\) elements in each tree, i.e., the time is \(O(\log m)\), which is also \(O(\log n)\) since \(m<n\). If \(x\) is in a component of size 1 (there is at least one such component), then the time for Find-Set\((x)\) is constant, i.e., not \(\Omega(\log n)\) or \(\Omega(\log m)\).

data.title: Choice of algorithm (4%)

Work and span (4%)

Consider the following parallel algorithm, which finds the maximum in an array \(A[1\!:\!n]\) by divide and conquer.

Assume that \(n = q-p+1\). What are the work and span of the algorithm?

Exactly one answer is correct, but you may select more than one if you are in doubt.
data.title: Work and span (4%)

metadata.distractor_rationale: Each recursive step splits the input into two halves and performs constant extra work. The recurrence for the work is \(T_1(n)=2T_1(n/2)+O(1)=\Theta(n)\). The span is determined by the longest chain of dependencies: \(T_\infty(n)=T_\infty(n/2)+O(1)=\Theta(\log n)\). The algorithm thus has linear work and logarithmic span.

data.stimulus:
Largest common prefix sum (12%)

For an array \(S[1\!:\!n]\), a prefix sum of \(S\) is defined as a number of the form \(\sum_{i=1}^jS[i]\), for \(j\in\{0,1,\ldots,n\}\). In this problem we are given three arrays \(A[1\!:\!n],B[1\!:\!n],C[1\!:\!n]\), all containing positive integers. We want to find the largest number \(x\) that is a prefix sum of each of \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\). In other words, it must be possible to write \(x\) as \(x=\sum_{i=1}^aA[i]=\sum_{i=1}^bB[i]=\sum_{i=1}^cC[i]\) for indices \(a,b,c\in\{0,1,\ldots,n\}\). Note that these indices \(a,b,c\) are allowed to be different.

a)  Let \(A=\langle 1,2,3,4\rangle\), \(B=\langle 3,2,3,4\rangle\) and \(C=\langle 1,1,1,4\rangle\). What is the largest common prefix sum? Briefly justify your answer.

metadata.sample_answer: The answer is \(3\), which can be written as the prefix sums \(1+2=3=1+1+1\) in \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\), respectively (we choose \(a=2\), \(b=1\), \(c=3\)). The only larger prefix sum of \(C\) is 7, which is not a prefix sum of \(A\) or \(B\).

data.stimulus: b)  Describe an algorithm that finds the largest common prefix sum. The input to the algorithm is the three arrays \(A,B,C\) and their size \(n\). You may write pseudocode, but a clear and precise description in text is also sufficient. To get full points, the running time must be \(O(n)\).

metadata.sample_answer: We can solve the problem with a greedy algorithm (but note that other solutions exist). We define variables \(x_A,x_B,x_C\), which are initially the sums of all numbers in \(A,B,C\), respectively. We also define indices \(a=b=c=n\). If \(x_A\) is strictly greater than \(x_B\) or \(x_C\), we subtract \(A[a]\) from \(x_A\) and subtract \(1\) from \(a\), and similarly if \(x_B\) or \(x_C\) is greater than one of the others. This corresponds to removing the last number from the prefix sum \(x_A\). When \(x_A=x_B=x_C\), we return this value. This happens after at most \(3n\) iterations, at which point we will have \(a=b=c=0\) and \(x_A=x_B=x_C=0\). Therefore the running time is \(O(n)\). In pseudocode it can be written as follows:

data.stimulus: c)  Argue that the algorithm always finds the correct answer.

metadata.sample_answer: We maintain the invariant that all three values \(x_A,x_B,x_C\) are greater than or equal to the solution \(x\). Since all numbers in \(A,B,C\) are positive, the invariant is true at the beginning. If one of \(x_A,x_B,x_C\), e.g. \(x_A\), is greater than another, we can thus conclude from the invariant that \(x_A\) is too large. Hence the invariant holds again after we have removed the last number \(A[a]\) from \(x_A\).

data.stimulus:
Algorithm analysis (12%)

Let \(\text{BinarySearch}(A, p, q, x)\) be the algorithm below, which implements binary search for \(x\) in an array \(A[p\!:\!q]\) in time \(O(\log n)\), where \(p\leq q\) and \(n = q-p+1\) is the number of elements, with \(n>1\). Assuming that \(A[p\!:\!q]\) contains integers sorted in nondecreasing order, \(\text{BinarySearch}(A, p, q, x)\) returns true if \(x\) is in \(A[p\!:\!q]\) and false otherwise.

An array \(A[1\!:\!n]\) is strictly bitonic if there exists an index \(i\) such that \(A[1\!:\!i]\) is increasing and \(A[i:n]\) is decreasing.

Example: \(A_1 = \langle 1, 2, 3, 5, 2, 1, 0\rangle\) is strictly bitonic because \(A_1[1\!:\!4] = \langle 1, 2, 3, 5\rangle\) is increasing and \(A_1[4:7] = \langle 5, 2, 1, 0\rangle\) is decreasing. \(A_2 = \langle 1, 2, 3, 5, 2, 2, 0\rangle\) cannot be strictly bitonic because it has two consecutive identical values.

a)  Give an example of a strictly bitonic array \(A[1\!:\!n]\) and an element \(x\) from \(A\) for which \(\text{BinarySearch}(A, 1, n, x)\) returns false (even though \(x\) is in \(A\)).

metadata.sample_answer: For \(A = \langle 3, 2, 1\rangle\) and \(x=1\), \(x\) is first compared with \(2\) and then with \(3\) in the next iteration.

data.stimulus:
Let \(\text{ReverseBinarySearch}(A, p, q, x)\) have the same functionality as \(\text{BinarySearch}\), except that \(A[p\!:\!q]\) is assumed to be sorted in reverse order (nonincreasing order). We now consider the following recursive algorithm:

b)  Write down a recurrence for the worst-case running time \(T(n)\) of \(\text{BTS2}\) on an input of length \(n\), and use it to derive an asymptotic upper bound on the running time. The analysis should be as precise as possible.

metadata.sample_answer: In the worst case, \(x\) is not in \(A[p\!:\!q]\), i.e., the algorithm returns only after both the binary search and the recursive call have been made. In this case the algorithm does constant work, one binary search on at most \(n/2\) elements (time \(O(\log n)\)), and one recursive call on at most \(n/2\) elements. This gives the recurrence \(T(n)=T(n/2)+O(\log n)\). It can be solved with the master method or with the substitution method, with the result \(T(n)=\Theta((\log n)^2)\).

data.stimulus: c)  Assume that \(A[1\!:\!n]\) is strictly bitonic. Argue that \(\text{BTS2}(A, 1, n, x)\) returns true if \(x\) is in \(A[1\!:\!n]\) and false otherwise.

metadata.sample_answer: Let \(A[1\!:\!n]\) be strictly bitonic with peak \(i\), i.e., \(A[1\!:\!i]\) is increasing and \(A[i:n]\) is decreasing. For a given interval \(A[p\!:\!q]\), the test \(A[mid] < A[mid+1]\) determines whether \(mid\) lies in the increasing or the decreasing part. If \(A[mid] < A[mid+1]\), then \(A[p\!:\!mid]\) is increasing, and it is correct to use \(\text{BinarySearch}\) to determine whether \(x\) is in \(A[p\!:\!mid]\). Otherwise \(A[mid+1\!:\!q]\) is decreasing, and it is correct to use \(\text{ReverseBinarySearch}\) to determine whether \(x\) is in \(A[mid+1\!:\!q]\). If \(x\) is not in the monotone half, it can only be in the other half, which is handled recursively. The interval is halved in each step, so by induction on the size of the interval the algorithm returns true if and only if \(x\) is in \(A[1\!:\!n]\). (The base case \(p=q\) is handled by lines 2–5.)
